newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle Atlantis set for Thursday launch.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle Atlantis set for Thursday launch.

text.p: The U.S. space shuttle Atlantis was set for a pre-dawn blastoff on Thursday after two minor technical problems were resolved, NASA officials said on Wednesday.
The shuttle was to soar aloft at 4:08 a.m. EDT (0808 GMT) to pick up U.S. astronaut Jerry Linenger from Russia's Mir space station and drop off his replacement, Mike Foale.
Launch pad workers at the shuttle's Florida launch site had overcome two minor technical glitches since the countdown began on Monday, shuttle test director Doug Lyons said.
Two electronic boxes that had shown strange readings during testing later appeared to be working properly, and some unexpected moisture in a rocket thruster had to be cleaned up.
The extra work slowed some launch pad preparations but liftoff remained on schedule.
"We are slightly behind, but during the course of the day we expect to make up that time and don't expect this to be an issue," Lyons told a news conference on Wednesday.
Loading of the space shuttle's rust-coloured strap-on tank with super-chilled liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen rocket fuel got under way at about 6.45 p.m. EDT (2245 GMT) on Wednesday.
The shuttle's crew of seven, which includes a Russian woman and a French astronaut from the European Space Agency, were to start taking their seats aboard Atlantis at about 1 a.m. EDT (0500 GMT).

Forecasters were optimistic the weather would cooperate during the shuttle's short seven-minute launch window. "Conditions look good for getting off the ground tomorrow," shuttle weather officer Ed Priselac said.
Atlantis was to dock with Mir on Friday night. Linenger, a 42-year-old U.S. Navy captain and medical doctor, has been working aboard the orbiting outpost since January.
His mission was marred by a brief but serious fire and a string of breakdowns in the station's life support systems.
"You and your crew went through some incredible difficulties," NASA administrator Daniel Goldin told Linenger in a telephone call to Mir on Wednesday.
The NASA chief assured Linenger the shuttle was on track to bring him home in time for the birth of his second child in June.
"Hopefully with good weather we'll get the shuttle off and I won't be in the dog house with your wife," Goldin joked.
The mission will be the space shuttle's sixth visit to Mir. The cash-strapped Russian space programme now relies on the U.S. shuttle to haul 40 percent of the station's deliveries.
Atlantis is carrying 4,000 lbs (1,814 kg) of supplies and equipment for the station's crew, including a new oxygen generator and repair gear to patch a leak in the station's cooling system.
Foale, a British-born astrophysicist, will have a four-month tour of duty on Mir. He will be the fifth U.S. astronaut to live and work aboard the station.
